sections.1:
This Blueprint Document section introduces the solution direction for Archlin’s Phase 1 supply management implementation. Archlin operates in specialty chemicals manufacturing and uses SAP S/4HANA as its ERP system. The business context for this implementation is driven by Archlin’s need to address poor inventory planning and to establish a more structured, system-supported planning capability for supply management.

The Phase 1 scope is focused on supply management, with relevant planning capabilities including supply planning, inventory planning, safety stock, replenishment, source-of-supply management, planning calendars, supply plan visibility, exception-based review, reporting, and scenario analysis. Within the available solution context, Maestro supports supply planning capabilities such as graphical representations of supply plans, constraint visibility, configurable reporting, supply plan versus actuals analysis, unit-of-measure conversion where conversion factors exist, multi-echelon stock replenishment requirements, safety and cycle stock methods, demand inputs that drive supply requirements, replenishment on and off dates through planning calendars, lot size adherence, total stock and available-to-promise visibility, product classification, safety stock calculations based on future days of demand, and source-of-supply prioritisation. These capabilities are relevant to Archlin’s objective of improving inventory planning discipline within the supply management scope.

The target solution for Archlin is expected to provide a planning environment in which supply plans, inventory requirements, replenishment parameters, and planning exceptions can be reviewed and managed with greater transparency. Supply plans can be represented graphically with drill links to constraint details, and reports can be configured to support supply planners. Supply plan versus actuals can be reported through waterfall analysis based on archived supply plans. Where approval processes are required, tracking approvals on the supply plan can be configured, and approvers can approve or reject a supply order with reason codes and comments. Alerts can be used to notify approvers or submitters based on a defined frequency when supply plans require action, are rejected, or are approved.

For Archlin’s inventory planning challenge, the solution context includes the ability to apply multiple stock level requirements, including safety stock and cycle stock. Several safety stock methods are available, and safety stock can also be calculated based on the current calculation. Cycle stock can be achieved through days-of-supply calculations. Safety stock can be calculated based on future days of demand, and minimum lot size can be respected. Product classification can be maintained based on product characteristics or parameters, and ABC classification will be done. Inventory Planning and Optimization can identify strategic safety stock inventory levels based on customer service levels, supply variability, forecast error and bias; however, Inventory Optimization is not considered in the initial implementation.

Archlin’s replenishment planning design is expected to use planning data and master data controls to generate feasible replenishment requirements. Planning calendars can be maintained to turn replenishment on or off at locations in the network. System-generated plans follow lot size values provided, including minimum, maximum, and multiple quantities. Users can modify lot size information, with changes reflected in real time at the predetermined point in time. Replenishment can be driven by demand and safety stock, and adjustments to replenishment around key dates may be handled by adjusting demand, safety stock, and, where required, pre-plan setup. Multiple sources of supply for a SKU can be managed using prioritisation, and multiple lead times for the same source of supply can be managed for different time periods or transportation modes with priorities defined. Time-phased part source functionality allows different sources of supply or lead times to be managed based on effective dates, and exceptional changes of sources can be made manually.

The implementation for Archlin will require integration and planning data alignment with SAP S/4HANA and any downstream or supporting planning processes within the defined Phase 1 scope. The available context states that cost and pricing information can be brought into Maestro and reports can be built based on that information. Standard cost, average selling price, customer contract price, and point-to-point transfer costs can be fed through integration, with transfer costs also maintainable while creating an inventory transfer within Maestro. Unit-of-measure conversion is possible when conversion factors between units of measure exist. Where demand inputs are required to drive supply requirements, demand that does not consume forecast can be loaded to drive supply requirements throughout the network.

Scenario planning is a key supporting capability for Archlin’s supply management implementation. The solution context supports setting up different scenarios with different sources to understand cost implications, performing what-if analysis, scoring and comparison, and committing scenarios into the baseline plan and budget. This capability is relevant for assessing supply disruptions, alternate sourcing networks, supply constraints, replenishment actions, and inventory impacts before committing changes to the operational plan.

Reporting, analytics, and exception management are expected to support Archlin’s planning outcomes by making supply and inventory issues more visible to planners and decision makers. Reports can be configured to support supply planning, supply plan versus actuals can be reported, and performance can be reported based on defined KPIs or measures. Total stock and available-to-promise quantity can be differentiated in reporting. Aged inventory information can be reported with a different on-hand type, while expiry is not considered in the initial implementation; if considered in a later release, reporting for expiry-related inventory is feasible. Quality status information such as released, quarantined, and rejected can be brought into Maestro if integrated with relevant systems.

The intended outcome of the Phase 1 implementation is to provide Archlin with a more structured supply management planning foundation that improves visibility into inventory requirements, replenishment plans, supply constraints, safety stock, stock availability, and source-of-supply decisions. The Blueprint will guide the detailed design, configuration, integration, testing, and deployment activities required to support Archlin’s supply management scope while maintaining alignment with the documented functional capabilities and implementation constraints.

sections.2:
Archlin’s expected benefits from the Phase 1 supply management implementation are aligned to the business need to address poor inventory planning within its specialty chemicals manufacturing environment. The solution direction should therefore focus benefit realization on measurable planning outcomes that connect supply management capabilities to shareholder value categories such as revenue, COGS, SG&A, and capital. Within the available source material, the relevant benefit framework links primary benefit metrics to planning capabilities and operational metrics, providing a structure for evaluating how improved supply management can support Archlin’s business objectives.

For revenue-related value, the benefit framework identifies lost sale reduction and forecast accuracy as primary benefit metrics. These are supported by capabilities such as Demand at Risk / Critical Path Analysis, Segmentation, Supply Allocation / Prioritization, and Single Level Safety Stock Recommendation. The associated metrics include Reduced Weeks of Supply, Increased Forecast Accuracy, Improved Projected OTIF, and # On Time to Commit / On Time to Request. For Archlin, these measures are relevant because poor inventory planning can affect the ability to align available and projected supply with demand priorities, although specific current-state Archlin baseline values are .

For COGS-related value, the benefit framework identifies planner efficiency / headcount increase avoidance as the primary benefit metric. Relevant capabilities include dashboards by role, ownership, scenario planning, collaboration, prioritized exception messages, end-to-end supply plans, supply network dashboards, critical constraints, standard processes, integrated supply network, and supply at risk. The associated metric identified in the source material is Improved Planning Cycle Time (MRP Latency). In Archlin’s Phase 1 supply management scope, this supports a more structured planning process by improving visibility, exception management, and planning responsiveness; however, specific targets, cycle-time baselines, and expected improvement levels are .

<IMAGE id="7621e142a076"/>

For SG&A-related value, the benefit framework identifies obsolete inventory reduction, inventory holding cost reduction, and expedited freight cost reduction as primary benefit metrics. The associated metrics include Inventory Targets Plan v Actual, Reduced Total Inventory Holding, Reduce Planned Excess & Expiring Inventory, # Unplanned Expedited Freight Actions, and Reduced Periods of Coverage. These measures are directly relevant to Archlin’s stated pain point of poor inventory planning, because they provide a way to evaluate whether supply management planning is improving inventory positioning, reducing excess and expiring inventory exposure, and helping manage inventory carrying impacts. Specific Archlin inventory levels, holding cost values, obsolete inventory exposure, expedited freight spend, and target reductions are .

For capital-related value, the benefit framework identifies one time inventory savings (WC) and asset productivity / capital utilization as primary benefit metrics. The related metrics include Reduce Obsolete Inventory, Improved Constraint Utilization, Increased Plan Adherence, and Improved Cumulative Lead Time Accuracy. For Archlin, these outcomes are important to the Phase 1 supply management objective because inventory planning quality is connected to working capital, constraint usage, plan adherence, and lead-time accuracy. The available source material does not provide Archlin-specific working capital targets, constraint utilization baselines, plan adherence baselines, or cumulative lead-time accuracy measures; these remain .

<IMAGE id="5829905bba04"/>

Qualitative benefits for Archlin should be understood through the same capability framework. Capabilities such as scenario planning, collaboration, prioritized exception messages, end-to-end supply plans, supply network dashboards, critical constraints, standard processes, integrated supply network, and supply at risk can help establish more consistent planning behavior and clearer visibility into supply management decisions. These qualitative benefits are particularly relevant where current poor inventory planning may require better exception-driven planning, improved prioritization, and a more integrated view of supply. The source material does not provide Archlin-specific qualitative baseline observations, user feedback, or process maturity assessments, so these are .

<IMAGE id="06ce320a5cff"/>

Overall, the Phase 1 benefit realization approach for Archlin should use the documented benefit framework to connect supply management capabilities with measurable business outcomes, while treating all Archlin-specific baselines, benefit targets, and quantified financial impacts as TBD or  until confirmed through project discovery and approved data sources. This ensures that the benefits remain grounded in Archlin’s actual business context, the SAP S/4HANA environment, and the defined Phase 1 focus on supply management without introducing unsupported assumptions.

sections.4.1:
The purpose of the Demand Planning process for Archlin is to generate, evaluate, and form consensus around the monthly Demand Plan for a definable period. The specific planning period for Archlin is TBD. This process is directly relevant to Archlin’s stated pain point of poor inventory planning, because the agreed demand signal becomes an input to downstream supply management activities in Phase 1 scope.

The Demand Planning process includes preparation of demand planning data, generation of a statistical forecast, consideration of external forecasts, review and adjustment of the unconstrained demand plan, and approval of a consensus demand plan. The final output is shared with Supply Planners as the Consensus Demand Plan, representing the unconstrained demand plan.

<IMAGE id="5e785938762f"/>

### Current State Context

Archlin operates in specialty chemicals manufacturing and uses SAP S/4HANA as its ERP system. The source documents identify poor inventory planning as a key pain point for Archlin. The current demand planning process detail specific to Archlin is otherwise .

### Process Purpose

The Demand Planning process is designed to support Archlin in:

- Generating a monthly Demand Plan for a definable planning period.
- Evaluating statistical and external forecast inputs.
- Forming consensus around the unconstrained demand forecast.
- Providing an agreed Consensus Demand Plan to Supply Planning.
- Supporting Phase 1 supply management by improving the quality of the demand signal used for downstream planning.

### Demand Planning Process Flow

Archlin’s Demand Planning process is structured around the following activities sourced from the uploaded process content:

- Data preparation
  - The Forecast Item is defined at the level where historical demand must be aggregated and where the Statistical Forecast is generated.
  - Historical data is cleansed before statistical forecast generation.
  - Cleansing considers demand for which there are no actuals, updates for causals, and adjustments to outliers.
  - If New Product Introduction or End of Life products exist, Phase-In or Phase-Out profiles are defined and added to the Forecast Item.

- Statistical forecast generation
  - The Statistical Forecast is generated as part of the Demand Planning process.
  - The generated forecast becomes one of the inputs used to develop the Consensus Demand Plan.

- External forecast upload and review
  - External forecasts can be uploaded, reviewed, and updated for consideration in developing the Consensus Demand Plan.
  - External forecasts are selected and uploaded by Forecast Category.
  - Forecast Categories are available through a workbook dropdown.
  - New Forecast Categories can be added through the solution enhancement process; planners cannot create Forecast Categories on their own.

- Demand Review
  - The Demand Review is held once a month, typically in week 2 of every month.
  - The purpose of the Demand Review is to align on the aggregated unconstrained Demand Plan, prioritise required decisions, prepare decision statements, compare the aggregate business plan to budget, gain visibility of volume assumptions, risks, and opportunities, and agree recommendations for the Supply Review.
  - The horizon of the plans considered in this process is 18-24 months.
  - Ahead of the Demand Review meeting, the Demand Planner generates the Statistical Forecast and uploads external forecasts, such as Customer Forecast and Manual Forecast.
  - Based on these inputs, the system provides the Unconstrained Demand Plan using defined ratios.
  - The Unconstrained Demand Plan is reviewed during the Demand Review meeting with the Product Manager and Business Manager.
  - Adjustments or overrides are made as required.
  - The outcome is the agreed Unconstrained Demand Plan.

- Consensus demand planning
  - Demand Planners and Product Managers collectively review demand volumes.
  - They review the system-generated Consensus Demand Plan based on assigned weightings.
  - They adjust or override the forecast for selected products where needed.
  - They approve the consensus demand forecast.
  - The final approved result is published and shared with Supply Planners as the Consensus Demand Plan, representing unconstrained demand.

### Demand Planning Data Inputs

The source Demand Planning process data includes the following inputs and sources. Where the source document referenced Maestro and ERP, the Archlin target system alignment is TBD except for SAP S/4HANA being identified as Archlin’s ERP system.

| Input | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Historical Labelling | Maestro |
| SKU master data | ERP |
| Data hierarchies | ERP |
| Forecast Item (product/location/customer) | Maestro |
| SoldTo and ShipTo Customer information | ERP |
| Product Status/Lifecycle information | Maestro |

### Solution Design Considerations

The solution design for Archlin’s Demand Planning process should support the following sourced capabilities:

- Define a demand plan process calendar, ownership, and cadence.
- Start process instances.
- Track and monitor process instances.
- Define Forecast Items at the level required for historical aggregation and statistical forecast generation.
- Cleanse historical demand data before forecast generation.
- Maintain Phase-In and Phase-Out profiles for New Product Introduction and End of Life products where applicable.
- Generate a Statistical Forecast.
- Upload, review, and update external forecasts by Forecast Category.
- Support Demand Review adjustments and overrides.
- Produce an agreed Unconstrained Demand Plan.
- Publish the approved Consensus Demand Plan to Supply Planning.

### Implementation Implications for Archlin

For Archlin’s Phase 1 supply management scope, the Demand Planning process provides the demand signal needed for supply review, balancing, replenishment, and inventory planning activities. The implementation should therefore ensure that demand inputs, forecast review steps, and consensus outputs are structured to support supply management execution.

Key implementation implications are:

- Archlin must define the demand planning calendar, ownership, and cadence.
- Archlin must confirm the definable monthly planning period for the Demand Plan.
- Archlin must confirm the Forecast Item structure, including product, location, and customer dimensions where applicable.
- Archlin must confirm which data elements are mastered in SAP S/4HANA and which are maintained in the planning solution.
- Archlin must define the external Forecast Categories required for the process.
- Archlin must define how adjustments and overrides are captured and approved during Demand Review.
- Archlin must confirm how the approved Consensus Demand Plan is transferred to downstream supply planning activities.

### Expected Outcomes

The expected outcomes of the Demand Planning process for Archlin are:

- A reviewed and agreed monthly Demand Plan for a definable period.
- An Unconstrained Demand Plan reviewed through the Demand Review process.
- A Consensus Demand Plan published to Supply Planners.
- Visibility of demand assumptions, risks, and opportunities.
- Improved demand signal quality to support Archlin’s Phase 1 supply management scope and address poor inventory planning.
sections.5:
Archlin’s Phase 1 supply management scope is centred on improving supply and inventory planning capabilities for its specialty chemicals manufacturing business. The current Archlin context identifies poor inventory planning as a key pain point, and the supply planning process must therefore provide a structured capability to align supply to the demand plan generated through the consensus demand planning process, replenish supply when inventory drops below defined safety stock levels, and identify, analyse, and resolve inventory issues such as projected late orders and stockouts. The detailed Archlin planning horizon, inventory target definitions, planning calendars, lead-time settings, and safety stock policies are TBD where not specified in the available source documents.

For Archlin, the Supply Planning process will support review of the system-generated supply plan and enable planners to firm orders based on lead time, as well as process ad-hoc inventory transfers when required within the short-term planning horizon. This is particularly relevant to Archlin’s inventory planning challenge, as the process must provide visibility to supply imbalances, including inventory shortfalls and excess inventory, based on the updated supply plan. The supply planner will analyse these imbalances, resolve bottlenecks and supply issues to the maximum possible extent, and then review slow-moving or obsolete inventory, black stock information, and other inventory-quality concerns where applicable. Specific Archlin definitions for SLOBS, black stock categories, target categories, and baseline scenarios used for inventory targets are TBD.

The solution design for Archlin will provide capabilities to identify parts with period-ending inventory values that are above or below targets, identify parts with periods-of-supply values that are above or below targets, and review Inventory Quality Ratio metrics to assess the quality of inventory. These capabilities are intended to enable exception-based supply and inventory management rather than relying only on reactive analysis. Archlin planners will be able to explore and simulate different options for resolving inventory exceptions, analyse the impact of proposed adjustments, collaborate with others to resolve exceptions, and review proposed adjustments before capturing them in Archlin’s SAP S/$HANA environment. The exact integration method, transaction ownership, approval workflow, and capture mechanism for adjustments in SAP S/$HANA are TBD.

The target Supply Planning process for Archlin will establish a feasible plan by considering material and capacity constraints, including labour capacity, production capacity, tank capacity, shipping constraints, and other constraints identified through the planning process. The objective is to support on-time delivery, inventory target achievement, and inventory projections while remaining aligned to the agreed demand plan. The process will also provide visibility of over-capacity and under-capacity conditions so that Archlin planners can take appropriate action. Where short-term demand plans require review, Archlin’s supply planning process will support the identification and resolution of related supply issues within the available planning scope.

The implementation approach for this section of Archlin’s Phase 1 blueprint is to define the supply planning and inventory exception management capabilities required to support supply management. This includes confirming the planning inputs, target categories, baseline scenario used for targets, inventory exception logic, periods-of-supply measures, inventory value target logic, and the roles that will execute planning actions. The source context notes that Inventory Planners and Master Schedulers are mapped to the Supply Planner role; the specific Archlin role mapping and named responsibilities remain TBD unless confirmed by Archlin. Required decisions and assumptions will need to be resolved during implementation so that the configured process reflects Archlin’s operating model and SAP S/$HANA planning data.

<IMAGE id="15a77c2812d0"/>

The expected outcome for Archlin is a supply management process that improves visibility to inventory exceptions, projected shortages, excess inventory, late supply, stockouts, and capacity-related constraints. By aligning supply to the consensus demand plan and enabling planners to evaluate exceptions against inventory targets, Archlin will be better positioned to make informed supply decisions and reduce the operational impact of poor inventory planning. The final business outcomes, target metrics, service-level expectations, inventory value targets, and quantified benefits are TBD because they are not specified in the available Archlin source documents.
sections.6.1:
Archlin’s Phase 1 technical architecture is focused on supply management and is intended to address the stated business pain point of poor inventory planning by enabling structured data exchange between Archlin’s SAP S/$HANA environment and the Kinaxis planning solution. The architecture for Archlin will support movement of supply-chain planning data from enterprise source systems into Kinaxis, with the detailed interface design, data objects, transfer cadence, and any outbound return flows to be confirmed during implementation where not yet available in Archlin source documents.

At a high level, the integration pattern for Archlin follows the established enterprise planning architecture in which data is extracted or collected from the ERP or other source systems, transformed into the format required by Kinaxis, and then made available for loading into the Kinaxis environment. The source context confirms that data movement into Maestro can be supported through tab-delimited text files and that integration architectures commonly include secure file-based transfer through an integration layer and data transfer components before loading into the Kinaxis database. For Archlin, SAP S/$HANA is the identified ERP system; the specific integration middleware, connector approach, detailed extract mechanism, and transformation ownership are TBD.

<IMAGE id="eed5d37ae32c"/>

The inbound integration flow for Archlin should therefore be understood as ERP source data originating from SAP S/$HANA, being extracted into the required file or integration format, passed through a secure transfer layer, and loaded into Kinaxis for supply management planning. The reference architecture describes a secure, multi-stage data transfer process using text files, a Data Transfer Client, firewalls, an FTP gateway, an FTP server, and the RapidResponse database. This pattern is relevant to Archlin’s implementation because it establishes the expected architectural controls around file movement, network boundaries, and controlled loading into the planning platform. The actual Archlin network zones, security controls, SFTP or FTP endpoint details, and RapidResponse or Maestro tenant configuration are TBD.

The outbound integration flow for Archlin is also to be defined based on the final approved design. The source material establishes that data load can happen in both directions: from ERP or other source systems through an integration tool into Kinaxis Maestro, and from Kinaxis Maestro through an integration tool back to ERP or other reporting systems. For Archlin, any outbound supply management results, planning outputs, reporting extracts, or closed-loop signals back to SAP S/$HANA or other Archlin systems are TBD unless separately confirmed in Archlin project documentation.

The implementation approach for Archlin should include confirmation of the technical components, data model changes, integration and automation tasks, and any closed-loop and reconciliation requirements. The architecture must define how Archlin’s SAP S/$HANA data is extracted, how it is transformed to the required Kinaxis format, how it is transferred securely, how Kinaxis loads are triggered and monitored, and how exceptions are reconciled. Where Archlin-specific file names, data objects, load frequencies, schedules, interface ownership, source tables, target tables, and validation rules are not present in the available source context, these items remain TBD and should be completed during detailed design.

The expected outcome of this architecture for Archlin is a controlled and repeatable data integration foundation for Phase 1 supply management. By establishing reliable inbound data feeds from SAP S/$HANA into Kinaxis, Archlin will have the technical basis required to improve supply planning visibility and support inventory planning processes. The solution will depend on accurate source extraction, agreed transformation logic, secure transfer, successful loading into Kinaxis, and defined reconciliation controls so that planning users can work from consistent supply-management data within the planning environment.
